29.title: Cato's last night
29.hook: at Utica in 46 BCE, refusing Caesar's pardon, Cato reads Plato on the soul through the night, and his ending is told honestly, not as a model
29.howItsDone: Many traditions ask people to reach out in despair and to watch over those who are struggling; today that includes crisis lines such as 988 in the US, open at any hour.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cleanthes carried water, and week four closed on his idea: no task is beneath a person who does it well. Day twenty-nine, and week five begins.

Week five is called Rome's hard nights, and it begins with the hardest. A word before we start: today's story ends in a death, and it's told carefully. North Africa, the city of Utica. Rome is tearing itself apart in civil war, and Julius Caesar has just won. On the losing side is Marcus Cato, a senator famous for being honest to the point of stubbornness, who had fought Caesar for years. Caesar is coming. And he is known for pardoning his enemies. Cato refuses to be pardoned.
screen: `ROME'S HARD NIGHTS.` → `UTICA, NORTH AFRICA.` → `CATO REFUSES A PARDON.`

segments.voice: Our source is Plutarch, writing generations later. He tells us Cato spent that last day making sure everyone else got out: arranging ships, calming the townspeople, helping others escape or make their peace with Caesar. That evening he had dinner with friends and argued philosophy, loudly, about whether only a good person is truly free. Then he went to his room and read Plato's Phaedo, the dialogue about the death of Socrates and the soul, late into the night. His son and his friends could see where his mind was going. They were frightened. They stayed close. They pleaded with him. And before morning, Cato ended his own life. Later Romans praised him for it, and some Stoics saw it as a free choice. This path doesn't tell it that way, and it isn't a model. Many traditions, Jewish, Christian, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist and others, teach against taking one's own life, and modern understanding sees much more going on in a night like that: exhaustion, despair, a mind that has narrowed until only one door seems open. What Plutarch's account does show, if you read it slowly, is the people around him. A son and friends who noticed, who tried, who wanted him to stay. That's the part to keep. Hard nights are real. The mind at 3am is not a reliable narrator. It tells you the dark is permanent. It isn't. Morning comes, and so do other doors. But you often can't see them alone. That's what people are for.

30.title: Seneca: life is long enough
30.hook: Seneca argues we are not given a short life but make it short by wasting it
30.howItsDone: Many people who follow Stoic practice review their day each evening, as Seneca described doing, noticing where their time and attention actually went.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Cato's last night, and the son and friends who tried to reach him. Reach out before morning stays true every night.

Where did the year go? I don't have time. Life is short. A Roman writer looked hard at that complaint and said no. Seneca: born in Spain, raised in Rome, Stoic philosopher, playwright, senator, and, awkwardly, an enormously rich man and adviser to the emperor Nero. A complicated man, who wrote a short essay still read today: On the Shortness of Life.
screen: `WHERE DID THE YEAR GO?` → `A ROMAN SAYS NO.` → `ON THE SHORTNESS OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Most people, he says, even great thinkers, grumble that nature is stingy, that life runs out just as we're getting ready to live it. Then he turns it over. We aren't given a short time; we waste a great deal of it. Life is long enough, and generous enough, for the greatest things, if the whole of it is well spent. Poured out on distractions, on chasing what doesn't matter, on other people's errands we never chose, it's gone at the end before we ever noticed it passing. His picture is money. Hand a fortune to a careless owner and it's gone in no time; hand a modest sum to a careful one and it grows. Life works the same way. His Latin is short enough to remember: vita, si uti scias, longa est. Life, if you know how to use it, is long. Now the awkward part. Critics in his own time pointed out that a man this rich, this close to power, was lecturing everyone else about what matters. He knew it, and answered, in another essay, that he was describing the good life, not claiming he'd reached it. Honesty or excuse, the essay has outlived the argument. And notice what he isn't saying. Not cram more in, be more productive. The opposite: stop giving your life away to things you never chose, and you'll find more of it than you thought.

31.title: The ledger of hours
31.hook: we guard our money closely and hand out our time to anyone who asks
31.howItsDone: People who follow Seneca's advice often keep an account of their time, as he told Lucilius he did, and deliberately protect some hours for what they value most.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Seneca, who said life isn't short, only wasted. Long enough, if used. Today, the ledger.

A stranger asks for twenty dollars, no reason. The answer is no, probably without a thought. A stranger asks for twenty minutes: a survey, a sales call, a meeting that could have been an email, a video that autoplays into the next. Those get handed over all day long. Seneca noticed the same strange double standard, in yesterday's essay. We guard our money. We give our time to anyone who asks.
screen: `TWENTY DOLLARS? NO.` → `TWENTY MINUTES? SURE.` → `WE GUARD THE WRONG THING.`

segments.voice: In the essay's third chapter, people won't let anyone take an inch of their land, Seneca says. One boundary dispute and they're off to court, with stones and weapons. But they let others walk right into their lives, and even invite them in. Nobody hands out their money; everybody hands out their life. Tight-fisted with property, wildly generous with the one thing it would be right to be stingy with: time. Then a clever move. He asks a man who's reached old age to go through the ledger. Take your years and subtract. How much went to a creditor, to a patron you had to flatter, to quarrels at home, to errands around the city? Subtract all that, and you have fewer years than you counted. In the first of his letters to his friend Lucilius, it's one line, in Richard Gummere's translation: "Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time." A house can be taken, money lost. Time is the one thing put in your hands alone, and the one thing nobody ever returns. He doesn't say never give it away. Friendship, service, love: those take hours, and they're worth it. His point is the ledger. Know where it goes. Choose where it goes. Guard at least one hour the way you'd guard your wallet.

32.title: Seneca in exile
32.hook: banished to Corsica, he writes to comfort his mother instead of asking for comfort
32.howItsDone: The consolation letter was a Roman genre for comforting the grieving; people still write in its spirit, reaching out to those who worry about them as well as those who grieve.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Seneca's ledger of hours. Time is the only property, and nobody gives it back.
screen: `THE LEDGER OF HOURS — TIME IS THE ONLY PROPERTY.`

segments.voice: Rome, the year 41. A new emperor, Claudius, has just come to power, and the palace is full of plots. Seneca, rising fast, famous, rich, is accused of an affair with the new emperor's niece. True or not, nobody can say now; many historians suspect politics. The sentence: exile to Corsica, a rocky island Romans thought of as the edge of nowhere. Back in Rome, his mother, Helvia, who'd already buried people she loved, now loses her son to an island. He could have written home asking for pity. He didn't.
screen: `ROME, THE YEAR 41.` → `ACCUSED, AND SENT AWAY.` → `A MOTHER LEFT BEHIND.`

segments.voice: He wrote to comfort her. The Consolation to Helvia is one of the strangest letters from antiquity: the exile consoling the one who stayed home. He admits he hesitated; it felt odd to offer comfort while being the reason she needed it. Then he gets to work. Don't grieve for me, he says; I'm not miserable. A place can't make a person unhappy. Wherever we go, the sky goes with us, and so does whatever good is in us. Then he turns to her life: the losses she's already carried, and how she carried them. He urges her back to the philosophy she'd only tasted, the studies her husband had once discouraged. And he points her to the people still around her: his brothers, the grandchildren, and her sister, who had cared for Seneca as a sick child. Lean on them. The honest footnote: from the same island he wrote a very different consolation, to a powerful official at court, full of flattery for the emperor, reading a lot like a plea to be brought home. Not a saint in a cave; a lonely man who wanted to go home. After eight years he was called back to Rome, and what waited there is tomorrow's story. But the letter to his mother is the part people keep. When your own life has gone wrong, you can still turn toward the person worrying about you, and comfort them.

33.title: Seneca's last hours
33.hook: ordered to die by Nero, he tells his friends he leaves them the one thing he has, the image of his life
33.howItsDone: Some people reflect on the legacy of character they hope to leave, sometimes by writing a short statement of how they want to be remembered and returning to it as a guide.

segments.voice: Yesterday: consolatio, the letter Seneca sent from exile to comfort his mother. Comfort the comforter.

A soldier arrives at a country house with the emperor's order: the man inside is to die. The man is Seneca. He came home from exile to tutor a boy named Nero; the boy became emperor, and for a few years Seneca helped steer the empire. Then Nero changed. Seneca tried to step away, even offering to hand back his fortune. Then a plot to kill Nero was uncovered. Whether Seneca was part of it, nobody knows. Nero didn't need to know.
screen: `A SOLDIER AT THE DOOR.` → `THE TUTOR AND THE EMPEROR.` → `A PLOT AGAINST NERO.`

segments.voice: The Roman historian Tacitus, writing some decades later, tells it plainly. Seneca, calm, asks for his will so he can leave gifts to his friends. The soldier refuses. So he turns to the friends around his table. Since he can't thank them as they deserve, he'll leave them the only thing he still has, and the most beautiful: the image of his life. Remember it, and they'll be known for good character and faithful friendship. His friends start weeping. Seneca, gently and then more firmly, asks where their philosophy has gone, all those years of preparing for exactly this. His wife, Paulina, is with him and wants to die with him. Tacitus says Nero, not wanting to seem too cruel, ordered her kept alive; she lived on some years, pale for the rest of her life, remembering him. Seneca died, as ordered. This isn't told to make death look noble. It's told for one line. The money, the house, the will: all of it could be taken. What was left was the image of how he'd lived. Not a statue, not even his writings: the picture of a life his friends would carry. And a question for any of us, long before the end. If the people who love you described the image of your life in one line, what would it be? Is it the line you'd choose?

34.title: Diogenes and the king
34.hook: Alexander offers him anything, and the Cynic asks him to stand out of his sunlight
34.howItsDone: The Cynics practiced radical simplicity, living with almost no possessions; some people today borrow a gentler version, cutting back on what they own and chase to make room for simple goods.

segments.voice: Yesterday: imago vitae, the image of a life, the one gift Seneca had left to give. After three heavy days, a lighter one.
screen: `IMAGO VITAE — THE IMAGE OF A LIFE.`

segments.voice: Corinth, Greece. Alexander, the young king of Macedon, not yet the conqueror he's about to become, comes to town, and everyone important rushes to congratulate him. One man doesn't come. So Alexander goes to find him, lying on the ground in the sun: an old man with a stick, a cloak and almost nothing else. The young king with an army stands over the man who owns nothing, and makes him an offer.
screen: `A YOUNG KING IN CORINTH.` → `EVERYONE RUSHES TO THE KING.` → `ONE MAN STAYS IN THE SUN.`

segments.voice: He was Diogenes of Sinope, the Cynic: one of the dog-like philosophers from Zeno's story, who owned nothing and said what they thought. Crates, the door-opener, is said to have learned from him. Our source is a different Diogenes, Diogenes Laërtius, a biographer writing centuries later. Same name, no relation. Alexander says: ask me for anything you want. Diogenes squints up and says: stand out of my light. That's it. Offered the world, he wanted the sun back. He lived like that on purpose. The stories say he slept in a big clay storage jar, walked around in broad daylight with a lamp, looking for a human being, and, asked where he was from, answered: I'm a citizen of the world. He wasn't always pleasant; the stories are full of rudeness and stunts. But there was a serious point underneath. One way to read this one: much of what people chase is a kind of shade, blocking a simple good already shining on them. And a strange ending. Plutarch says that as Alexander walked away, his officers laughing at the old man, the king said: if I weren't Alexander, I would be Diogenes. Maybe the king saw the one thing an empire couldn't give the Cynic, because he already had it: the light.
screen: `DIOGENES OF SINOPE, THE CYNIC.` · `ASK ME FOR ANYTHING.` · `A LAMP IN BROAD DAYLIGHT.` · `IF I WEREN'T ALEXANDER.` · then, large: `STAND OUT OF MY LIGHT.`

segments.voice: If there's sunlight near you, sit or stand in it; if not, a lamp or the memory of sun on your face will do. Close your eyes and feel the warmth: nothing is being offered, and nothing is needed. When a want or a worry steps in front of it, notice the shade, and let it move aside.

35.title: Diogenes throws away his cup
35.hook: seeing a child drink from cupped hands, he tosses away his last possession
35.howItsDone: Many traditions practice voluntary simplicity, from the Cynics and monastic vows of poverty to modern decluttering, giving away what isn't needed so that it can serve someone else.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diogenes and the king: stand out of my light, because some good things are already shining. Today closes week five.
screen: `DIOGENES AND THE KING — STAND OUT OF MY LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Somewhere near you there's a junk drawer. Old chargers for phones nobody owns anymore. Keys to nothing. A takeout menu from a place that closed. Now meet a man whose whole house fits in a small bag over his shoulder: a cloak, a stick, a bag, and a cup for drinking. That's Diogenes, the Cynic who told Alexander to move out of his sunlight. One day he watched a child get a drink of water, and lost one more thing.
screen: `A DRAWER FULL OF KEYS TO NOTHING.` → `A CLOAK, A STICK, A BAG, A CUP.` → `A CHILD, DRINKING.`

segments.voice: Diogenes Laërtius tells it like this. Diogenes sees a child drinking water from his cupped hands. He pulls the cup out of his bag and throws it away, saying something like: a child has beaten me at living simply. The same source tells a twin story: seeing a boy who'd broken his bowl eat lentils from a hollowed piece of bread, he threw away his bowl too. Notice who the teacher is. Not a philosopher: a child, someone who didn't know you're supposed to need a cup. The man who owned almost nothing still found something to put down. Careful, though. This is a story about choosing to carry less, not one that makes poverty romantic. Diogenes chose his life, and plenty of people in his world, and ours, don't get to choose. The Cynics weren't after hardship for its own sake. They were after freedom. One way to put their point: every thing you own also owns a little of you. It needs storing, protecting, repairing, worrying about. Put it down and your hands are free. That closes week five: Rome's hard nights, Cato, Seneca on a life long enough, his consolatio to his mother from exile, imago vitae in his last hours, Diogenes in the sun, and a cup thrown away because a child knew better. Hard stories, most of them, each asking the same quiet question: when everything else is taken, or given away, what's left? Tomorrow, a new week, and a very different teacher: a wise fool.
screen: `A CHILD DRINKS FROM HIS HANDS.` · `THE TEACHER IS A CHILD.` · `CHOSEN, NOT ROMANTIC.` · `WEEK FIVE: WHAT'S LEFT?` · then, large: `LESS TO CARRY.`

segments.voice: Take a slow tour of your home in your mind: the closet, the drawers, the shelf you never look at. Find one thing you don't use and wouldn't miss, something someone else could use, and picture handing it to them. Then notice how your hands feel.
